strengths: Introduces a comprehensive taxonomy of 13 score functions for identifying inactive attention heads, going beyond the narrow attention-weight-only definitions (e.g., attention sink/dormant head) used in prior work, by also considering value vectors and head outputs.

Rigorously verifies claimed inactivity through actual model interventions (zeroing heads) and measuring downstream task accuracy (MMLU) rather than relying solely on proxy scores, which is a meaningful methodological improvement over prior work that only inspected attention weights.
Broad empirical coverage: 14 pretrained models across 3 model families (Llama, OLMo-2, Qwen2.5) and multiple scales (0.5B to 14B), enabling cross-family and cross-scale analysis.

Interesting and fairly convincing findings: Avg Head Output Norm consistently outperforms attention-weight-based scores across models, and reliance on first-token-attention-sink metrics underestimates inactive heads by ~7%.

Additional insights beyond the main result, e.g., minimal impact of finetuning (SFT/DPO/RLHF) on attention score distributions and limited effect of scale on attention behavior except at very large scale, add value to the paper's contribution.
Extensive appendix material (full results per model/score function, PyTorch implementations, dataset/model details) supports reproducibility and transparency.
weaknesses: The core contribution is largely empirical/observational: proposing threshold-based heuristic scores and measuring correlations/AUC, without a deeper theoretical grounding or principled derivation of why 'Avg Head Output Norm' should be the most reliable indicator of true inactivity beyond the empirical AUC ranking.

The paper explicitly disclaims efficiency implications ('our focus is strictly on understanding... not... efficient inference'), which limits the practical significance of the findings; no throughput/latency/memory benefits are demonstrated despite motivating discussion of KV cache/compression relevance.

The evaluation of 'inactivity' is restricted to a single downstream benchmark (MMLU), which may not fully capture behaviors relevant to generation-based tasks, long-context reasoning, or other benchmarks; results could be benchmark-specific (as shown by the FineWeb-Edu vs. MMLU distribution shift in the appendix, e.g., Fig. 9).

Thresholds for classifying heads as inactive are chosen via arbitrary quantile-based heuristics (p in {0,5,...,30}), and the maximum percentage of heads considered is capped at 30%, which may bias comparisons between scoring functions and make the reported '12% average inactive heads' somewhat sensitive to these design choices.

Precision/IoU agreement between score functions is generally low (max IoU 0.58, max precision 0.73), indicating substantial disagreement among the proposed 13 functions; while framed as evidence of measuring 'different aspects,' this also raises concerns about the robustness/validity of any single score as ground truth for 'true' inactivity.

The model intervention approach zeros heads statically per evaluation (using thresholds computed on MMLU inputs) rather than fully dynamically per input in a way that could be deployed, and it's unclear how sensitive the results are to the specific 100 FineWeb-Edu samples used to determine IoU/precision comparisons.
Figures throughout (e.g., Fig. 2, 3, 5, 6, 8) are dense and difficult to read at normal resolution, with small labels, making it hard to verify claims visually.

Limited novelty in the general idea of head pruning/redundancy (well-established since Voita et al. 2019, Michel et al. 2019); the paper's novelty rests mainly on the specific choice and combination of score functions and their systematic empirical comparison, which is a comparatively incremental contribution.

The claim of finetuning having 'little to no effect' is based on only a few finetuning setups (OLMo-2 SFT/DPO/RLHF and a few Instruct variants), which may not generalize to more diverse finetuning regimes (e.g., heavy domain adaptation, continual pretraining, or larger-scale RLHF).

strengths: Proposes a reasonably comprehensive taxonomy of 13 score functions spanning attention weights, value vectors, and head outputs, moving beyond the narrow 'attention sink' definition of inactivity used in prior work (e.g., Guo et al., Gu et al.).
Conducts a large-scale empirical study across 14 pretrained models spanning 3 model families and multiple scales (0.5B-14B), which gives some breadth to the analysis.

Directly verifies claimed 'inactive' heads via model intervention (zeroing heads) and measuring downstream MMLU accuracy degradation, rather than relying purely on proxy scores — an important methodological improvement over prior score-only characterizations.

Provides useful negative results/insights, e.g., that attention-weight-based sink metrics (AWFT) systematically underestimate inactive heads by ~7% relative to output-norm-based metrics, and that finetuning barely changes attention behavior.

Includes fairly extensive appendix material (full per-model curves, score distributions, Wasserstein distance matrices, PCA of attention matrices) and released code snippets, aiding reproducibility to some degree.
weaknesses: The core contribution is largely a combination/extension of existing, well-known quantities (attention entropy, value-vector norm, head-output norm) into a taxonomy, rather than a fundamentally new technique; the individual score functions are simple and largely incremental relative to cited prior work (Guo et al. 2024a/b, Gu et al. 2025).

Verification of 'inactivity' relies solely on 5-shot MMLU accuracy; this is a narrow proxy that may not reflect the true functional role of a head (e.g., in generation quality, long-context reasoning, or other benchmarks). No perplexity or generation-quality evaluation is reported, despite this being a more direct/faithful test of whether head outputs are truly negligible.

The threshold selection procedure (choosing per-model, per-score-function quantiles to maximize the percentage of heads zeroed while staying within 1% of baseline accuracy, Table 2) is essentially a post-hoc search over thresholds on the same evaluation set used for reporting results, raising concerns about overfitting/selection bias in the headline '12% of heads are inactive' statistic; there is no held-out validation of these thresholds on unseen tasks.

Comparisons with prior 'redundant head' literature (Voita et al. 2019; Michel et al. 2019; Li et al. 2021) are only discussed qualitatively; no direct quantitative comparison with these iterative/optimization-based pruning approaches is provided in the intervention experiments, despite these being natural and stronger baselines beyond the simplistic AWFT and random baselines actually used.

Scale of models studied tops out at 14B parameters, and the claim that 'attention behavior is more invariant to scale until large sizes' is drawn from only 5 models within a single family (Qwen2.5), which is a fairly weak evidentiary basis for a generalizable scaling claim.

No quantification of actual computational/efficiency benefits (e.g., wall-clock speedup, FLOPs reduction, memory savings) despite the paper repeatedly motivating the work via efficiency and computational redundancy; the practical value of the findings for real inference speedups is left entirely unaddressed.

Several figures (e.g., Figs 3, 5, 8) are visually dense with very small illegible labels, making it difficult to verify some of the more nuanced claims (e.g., per-model ranking details, Wasserstein similarity patterns) without access to larger versions.

Statistical robustness is unclear: experiments appear to use a single sample of FineWeb-Edu sequences and a single evaluation pass per model/threshold without reported variance, error bars, or multiple seeds, making it hard to assess the significance of observed differences between score functions.

The finding that finetuning induces 'little to no change' in attention behavior is based on only a handful of finetuned model pairs (OLMo-2 SFT/DPO/Instruct, a few Instruct variants), which may not generalize across finetuning methods, datasets, or larger behavioral changes such as RLHF-induced safety tuning.

strengths: Proposes a comprehensive taxonomy of 13 score functions spanning three complementary aspects of attention heads (attention weights, value vectors, head outputs), moving beyond prior work that relied solely on attention-weight-based 'sink' heuristics.

Provides direct causal verification of inactivity via model interventions (zeroing head outputs) and measuring downstream MMLU accuracy, rather than relying only on correlational/threshold-based classification, which strengthens the validity of the claims.
Evaluates across 14 pretrained models spanning 3 model families (Llama, OLMo-2, Qwen2.5) and multiple scales, supporting reasonably broad empirical claims about generality of findings.

The finding that first-token attention-sink-based metrics underestimate inactive heads by ~7% and that average head output norm is a more model-agnostic and effective indicator is a useful and actionable insight for the community (e.g., for KV-cache/pruning research).
Additional analyses (finetuning invariance, scale effects within Qwen2.5 family, score distribution similarity via Wasserstein distance) add depth and provide interesting secondary findings.
Reasonable reproducibility support: pseudocode/PyTorch listings for key scoring functions, dataset/model details, and extensive appendix with full per-model results.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single downstream benchmark (MMLU) for verifying inactivity via intervention; conclusions about 'maintaining accuracy' may not generalize to other tasks (e.g., generation, reasoning, long-context tasks) where head removal effects could differ substantially.

Thresholds for each score function appear to be selected using score distributions computed on MMLU itself, and then heads are zeroed and re-evaluated on MMLU, raising a possible circularity/data-leakage concern that could inflate reported "heads maintainable within 1% accuracy" numbers.

The paper motivates the work partly via computational/efficiency redundancy (e.g., KV-cache reduction, compression) but never actually measures wall-clock speed, FLOPs, or memory savings from removing identified heads, leaving the practical efficiency implications unverified.

No comparison against existing head-pruning/importance-scoring baselines (e.g., Michel et al. 2019, Voita et al. 2019, or more recent KV-cache compression heuristics) in the intervention experiments beyond a random baseline and AWFT, making it hard to judge how much of an advance this represents over established pruning criteria.

Individual scoring functions are largely straightforward norm/entropy statistics; while the taxonomy and systematic comparison is a useful organizing contribution, the technical novelty of any single score function is incremental relative to prior work (e.g., Guo et al. 2024a/b, Gu et al. 2025).

Some figures (e.g., Figure 3 rank heatmap, Wasserstein distance matrices in Figures 5/8) are small and difficult to parse, and the paper doesn't report confidence intervals/variance for the MMLU accuracy curves, making it harder to judge robustness of the reported thresholds.

The claim that finetuning causes 'little to no change' in attention behavior is based only on a few finetuning variants (SFT/DPO/RLHF-style checkpoints of a small set of models) and Wasserstein distance on score distributions, which is a fairly indirect/aggregate measure that may mask localized but functionally important changes.

strengths: Thorough empirical study across 14 models from 3 model families (Llama, OLMo-2, Qwen2.5), including base, SFT, DPO, and instruct variants, providing broad coverage for claims about generalizability.

Introduces a reasonably comprehensive set of 12 (13 with appendix variant) score functions spanning attention weights, value vectors, and head outputs, motivated by a clear conceptual gap in prior work (that attention-weight-only definitions of 'dormant' heads miss cases where near-zero output arises from convex combinations of small value vectors).

Verification via actual model intervention (zeroing heads and measuring MMLU/PIQA/WinoGrande accuracy) rather than relying solely on proxy scores, which strengthens the causal claim that identified heads are truly inactive rather than just exhibiting a particular attention pattern.

Useful negative result: shows that the previously proposed 'Avg Weight of First Token' / dormant-head criterion (Guo et al., 2024a; Gu et al., 2025) substantially underestimates inactive heads and is unstable across datasets (Figure 5), which is a valuable corrective to prior literature.

Good use of appendix ablations (circuit-based head-output definition, additional benchmarks, sequence-length dependence, layer-wise analysis, PCA of attention matrices) that bolster robustness of the main claims.

The finding that fine-tuning (SFT/DPO/RLHF) barely changes attention score distributions, and that scale effects only emerge at larger sizes, are interesting observations with potential downstream implications for interpretability and efficient inference research.
weaknesses: The core methodology reduces to threshold-based univariate score functions with dynamically chosen thresholds per model/dataset; the choice of thresholds (percentile-based, capped at 30% of heads) is somewhat arbitrary and the paper does not deeply justify why 30% or the specific quantile grid was chosen, raising concerns about cherry-picking favorable operating points for the 'best' method.

Evaluation is restricted to single-forward-pass, log-likelihood-style MC benchmarks (MMLU/PIQA/WinoGrande); the more practically relevant case of open-ended generation is explicitly left as future work, limiting the practical significance of the 'computational redundancy' framing emphasized in the abstract/intro.

The headline claim of only 1% accuracy degradation while zeroing >12% of heads is aggregated/best-case across many score-function and threshold combinations per model (Table 2 picks the best score function per model post-hoc); it is unclear how a practitioner would select the right score function and threshold a priori without access to ground-truth accuracy, undermining the practical utility of the method beyond analysis.

AHON (the winning score function) requires computing the actual head output, so as acknowledged in the limitations, it cannot be used to skip computation for inference speedups — the main practical motivation given in the abstract/intro (computational redundancy, efficient inference) is therefore not actually realized, and the contribution is primarily analytical/descriptive rather than enabling any new efficient method.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are reported as point percentages/accuracy drops without confidence intervals, variance across seeds, or significance testing, making it hard to assess whether differences between score functions (e.g., 12.18% vs 4.61%) are robust or within noise, especially given the complex, non-monotonic accuracy curves shown in Figure 10 (e.g., large jagged discontinuities for some models/score functions).

The novelty of the paper is somewhat incremental: it largely extends existing observations about attention sinks/dormant heads (Guo et al. 2024a; Gu et al. 2025) by adding a few additional simple norm-based statistics and an intervention-based validation protocol, rather than proposing fundamentally new theory or a new efficient architecture/algorithm.

The paper's contribution regarding 'model scale' and 'fine-tuning' effects on attention behavior is based on Wasserstein distance heatmaps with fairly qualitative/visual interpretation (e.g., 'dark block diagonal pattern') rather than quantitative statistical tests, and the sample of model families/scales is small (mainly Qwen2.5 for the scale analysis), limiting generalizability of these secondary claims.

IoU/precision values between score functions (Figure 2) are computed on a single model (Llama-3.1-8B) and 100 sequences, which is a fairly narrow analysis to support the general claim that 'no score function is effectively the same as another' across all models studied.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across 14 pretrained models spanning 3 model families (Llama, OLMo-2, Qwen2.5) and multiple scales, which is more comprehensive than prior single-model studies of dormant/attention-sink heads.

The paper proposes a reasonably broad taxonomy of 12 score functions covering attention weights, value vectors, and head outputs, moving beyond the attention-weight-only view of prior work (e.g., Guo et al. 2024a; Gu et al. 2025).

Model intervention experiments (zeroing heads and measuring MMLU/PIQA/WinoGrande accuracy) provide a more direct verification of 'inactivity' than simply thresholding scores, which is methodologically sound.
Useful negative result: showing that Avg Weight of First Token underestimates inactive heads and is unstable across datasets/layers, which is a legitimate critique of prior heuristics.

Thorough appendix with additional normalization strategies, circuit-based head-output ablation, sequence-length analysis, and PCA visualization of attention sinks, suggesting a careful and diligent experimental effort.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core contribution is largely a combinatorial sweep of simple, previously-known quantities (attention entropy, value norm, output norm) with threshold-based classification; there is no new theoretical framework or mechanistic explanation for why output-norm-based heads are inactive.

The headline results (e.g., '12% of heads are inactive,' 'AHON best for 8/14 models') are highly sensitive to the arbitrary choice of thresholds/quantiles (capped at 30% of heads, 7 threshold levels), and the paper does not convincingly argue these numbers are meaningful beyond the specific experimental protocol chosen.

The practical motivation (efficiency, KV-cache reduction) is undercut by the authors' own admission that AHON requires computing the full head output first, making it unusable for actual compute savings — this significantly weakens the significance/impact of the central finding.

Evaluation is restricted to single forward-pass, log-likelihood multiple-choice benchmarks (MMLU, PIQA, WinoGrande); the authors acknowledge that generation-based evaluation (where errors compound) is not tested, which is a major gap given real-world LLM usage is generative.

The scientific claims are largely correlational/descriptive (e.g., 'finetuning causes little change in attention,' 'scale matters only at large sizes') without causal analysis or deeper investigation into why these patterns emerge, limiting the depth of insight offered.

Overlap and redundancy analysis (IoU/precision in Fig. 2) shows scores are only moderately distinct (max IoU 0.58), yet the paper still treats all 12 as meaningfully different without stronger justification for why nearly a dozen heuristics are needed rather than 2-3 well-motivated ones.

The framing as being 'the first to systematically evaluate' inactive heads overstates novelty given substantial prior work on head pruning/importance (Voita et al. 2019; Michel et al. 2019; Guo et al. 2024a) that already established zeroing/removal-based verification, even if at a smaller scale.

No error bars, statistical significance testing, or variance analysis for the accuracy degradation curves and percentage-of-heads-zeroed numbers, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported gains (e.g., '+18%' improvements for OLMo-2 models).

strengths: Broad and thorough empirical evaluation across 14 pretrained models spanning 3 model families (Llama, OLMo-2, Qwen2.5) and multiple benchmarks (MMLU, PIQA, WinoGrande), providing strong external validity for the claims.

Novel and important methodological contribution: verifying identified 'inactive' heads via actual model interventions (zeroing outputs and measuring downstream accuracy) rather than relying solely on proxy score functions, addressing a real gap in prior work (Guo et al. 2024a; Gu et al. 2025) that only inspected attention weights.

Systematic exploration of 12 (13 with appendix variant) score functions spanning attention weights, value vectors, and head outputs, with IoU/precision analysis showing these functions capture genuinely different head subsets rather than redundant signal.

Interesting and well-supported findings with practical implications: Avg Head Output Norm (LN) is the most model-agnostic and effective score, prior 'attention sink' based definitions substantially underestimate inactive heads (missing ~7% on average), finetuning barely changes attention behavior, and scale effects emerge mainly at large model sizes.

Strong reproducibility effort: PyTorch code listings for key score functions, detailed model/dataset documentation, extensive appendix with additional datasets, normalization strategies, circuit-based head-output ablation, and sequence-length/context-dependency analyses.

Honest and thoughtful discussion of limitations (single-forward-pass focus, computational overhead of the best score function, generation vs. log-likelihood evaluation) rather than overselling practical efficiency gains.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely analytical/empirical (simple thresholding of hand-designed scalar statistics) rather than a new algorithm or architecture; novelty is incremental relative to Guo et al. (2024a) and Gu et al. (2025), mainly extending the set of measured quantities.

No comparison against stronger/learned head-importance or pruning baselines (e.g., Michel et al. 2019, Voita et al. 2019, gradient/Taylor-based importance scores), which would better contextualize how good simple norm-based thresholds really are.

The chosen 1%-accuracy-drop criterion and percentile-based threshold sweeps (up to 30%) are somewhat arbitrary, and there is limited analysis of joint/combined criteria across multiple score functions simultaneously.

The paper's own results (Section 4.4, App. A.5) show that inactivity is highly context- and sequence-length-dependent, which raises questions about how stable/generalizable the headline '12% inactive' statistic actually is beyond the specific single-forward-pass MC-evaluation setting studied.

Practical efficiency motivation is undercut by the admission that the best-performing score function (AHON) requires computing the head output itself, making it unclear whether real inference speedups are achievable, weakening the significance of the 'efficiency' framing.

Analyses of score-distribution similarity (Wasserstein distance) for finetuning/scaling conclusions are descriptive/correlational without deeper causal or mechanistic grounding, and lack statistical significance testing across models/functions.
